nodes.title: Release gate: a ticket whose work merged must not still be open in tasks.json
nodes.prompt:
WHY: MTIX-65's fix merged in the first working session (157626a) and its ticket sat OPEN for days. Nobody noticed until the tracked tasks.json was read by eye before a gate report. Bookkeeping lag is invisible by construction — nothing fails, the code is right, only the record is wrong — and the record is what a release report is built from. A gate makes it impossible to carry into a release.

THE RULE, validated against all of main's history before proposing it:
A ticket named in a commit's CONVENTIONAL-COMMIT SCOPE must not be 'open' in .mtix/tasks.json.

  fix(backup)(MTIX-65): ...       -> MTIX-65 must not be open
  feat(relay)(MTIX-64.3): ...     -> MTIX-64.3 must not be open
  fix(MTIX-62): ...               -> MTIX-62 must not be open

WHY THE SCOPE POSITION, NOT ANY MENTION: I measured both.
  - Any MTIX-* anywhere in the subject: 184 tickets, 179 done, 4 cancelled, 1 OPEN — and that one is a FALSE POSITIVE. The commit is 'chore: close MTIX-2.3.1 (streaming import decode) + open MTIX-2.3.2 (bounded-memory JSONL)': it CREATED MTIX-2.3.2, it did not implement it. A gate that reds on ticket-creation commits would be re-run-and-ignore within a week.
  - Scope position only: 144 tickets, 144 done, ZERO violations across the whole history. Verified it still matches fix(backup)(MTIX-65) — the case that motivated this — and rejects the creation commit, 'chore: close MTIX-60', and merge commits.
So the discriminator is not a heuristic about wording; it is the repo's own commit convention, where work-landing commits put the ticket in the scope and prose mentions do not.

WHY 'open' AND NOT 'not done': in_progress is legitimate — an epic accrues commits while more work is coming, which is exactly how the FR-21 children were worked. 'open' means nobody has even claimed it, so a merged code commit naming it in scope is unambiguously a record that fell behind. Choosing the tighter predicate is what keeps the gate at zero false positives.

SCOPE:
- A checker that reads .mtix/tasks.json and git log, applies the rule, and exits non-zero listing each offending ticket with the commit that landed its work and the command that fixes it (mtix done <id>).
- Wire into CI so it runs on every push, and into the release path so no tag can be cut over a stale record.
- Bound the history it scans so the job stays fast and so a ticket cancelled long ago cannot resurrect the gate: scan since the last tag, with the full-history mode available behind a flag for an audit.
- Tests: the rule matches a scope-position ref; ignores a prose mention; ignores a ticket-creation commit; ignores merge commits; passes when the ticket is done, in_progress or cancelled; fails when it is open. Red-first.

OUT OF SCOPE: inferring completion from anything other than ticket status; touching tasks.json automatically (the export is written by mtix itself, and a gate that edits the thing it audits is not a gate).
nodes.acceptance: A checker exists, runs in CI on every push, and fails the build when a ticket named in a commit's scope is open in tasks.json. It reports the ticket, the commit, and 'mtix done <id>'. Zero false positives against current main history (verified: 144 scope-referenced tickets, all done). Unit tests cover match/no-match for scope refs, prose mentions, creation commits and merge commits, and status handling for open/in_progress/done/cancelled — each observed failing first. make lint-go clean.
nodes.creator: cli

nodes.title: TestPruneSnapshots_FlagsStaleOnesWithoutRemovingThem is time-of-day dependent: injected clock compared against a real file mtime
nodes.prompt:
OBSERVED: internal/relay/bootstrap test fails with 'expected: 30, actual: 29' when run after ~12:00 UTC and passes before it. Found while running the full suite for MTIX-74; it passed earlier the same day and failed hours later with no code change between.

ROOT CAUSE, same class as MTIX-70: half the comparison is injected and half is not. StaleSnapshots derives a snapshot's age from the FILE'S mtime — the real wall clock at the moment the fixture wrote it — while the test passes Now = fixedTime.AddDate(0,0,30), where fixedTime is 2026-08-23T12:00:00Z. Run at 14:00 UTC the age is 29.92 days, and int() truncation makes that 29.

THE CODE IS RIGHT; THE TEST IS WRONG. StaleSnapshots must use the medium's own timestamp: a snapshot file carries no wall clock of its own, and a remote publisher's clock is not something local retention should trust — the same reasoning that puts ModTime on retention.Segment. What is wrong is a test asserting an EXACT day count against an mtime it never controlled.

FIX: make the fixture control both sides — set the snapshot's mtime explicitly (os.Chtimes) so the age is exact and deterministic, rather than loosening the assertion to a range. A range would hide the truncation behaviour the test is actually pinning; controlling the input keeps the assertion at full strength. Same principle as the MTIX-70 ruling: do not weaken the claim, pin the input.

I INTRODUCED THIS in MTIX-64.7 (merge 10061e3) and it is on main now, so main's CI would fail if re-run after midday UTC. It passed its own merge run only because that run happened before the boundary — which is exactly why time-of-day flakes are worth a ticket rather than a quiet edit.

ALSO CHECK while fixing: other tests I added that mix an injected clock with a real filesystem timestamp. retention's prune tests construct Segment.ModTime directly and are safe; cmd/mtix's relayLastSeen reads real mtimes but asserts no exact age. Confirm nothing else compares an injected Now against an uncontrolled mtime.
nodes.acceptance: The test passes at any time of day — verified by running it with the clock's effect reproduced (an mtime set to a known instant), not merely by running it once. The assertion stays an exact day count rather than a range. No other test compares an injected clock against an uncontrolled file mtime. internal/relay/bootstrap green; make lint-go clean.
nodes.creator: cli

nodes.title: DiscardLocal strands hook_dispatch_cursor and hook_dispatch_ledger above the wiped journal
nodes.prompt:
Found while fixing MTIX-66 (same function, same defect class, same transaction).

DiscardLocal (internal/store/sqlite/sync_reconcile.go) wipes sync_events but leaves every table keyed to sync_events.rowid. MTIX-66 fixed the three inbox tables. The hook dispatch pair has the identical shape and is NOT yet fixed.

VERIFIED EMPIRICALLY, not inferred. A probe test seeded each candidate table, ran DiscardLocal, and counted surviving rows. Result: agent_inbox_cursor, agent_inbox_ack, inbox_deliveries, hook_dispatch_cursor, hook_dispatch_ledger and relay_push_cursor all STRANDED (rows survived); relay_ingest_cursor cleared (it tracks per-peer remote relay sequences, not local rowids, so it is correctly untouched). Journal tail after discard = 0.

WHY IT BITES. sync_events declares event_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY -- no INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT -- so there is no sqlite_sequence entry and rowids are NOT monotonic across a full DELETE. After the wipe the next insert takes rowid 1 again. Every surviving cursor/ledger row therefore sits above the entire new journal.

CONSEQUENCE, hook side:
- hook_dispatch_cursor is the scan floor: "everything at or below the floor is fully dispatched". Left at the old tail, the tail scan starts past the whole new journal, so NO hook fires for anything journaled after a discard-local until the journal grows back past the old tail. Silent: no error, no log, hooks simply never fire. This is the wake-agent path -- a coordination stall with no symptom.
- hook_dispatch_ledger rows pre-mark (hook, seq) pairs as already dispatched, so even a correct floor would skip the unrelated new events that reuse those rowids.

FIX SHAPE. Add DELETE FROM hook_dispatch_cursor and DELETE FROM hook_dispatch_ledger to the same statement list in the same tx as the journal wipe, immediately after the inbox deletes MTIX-66 added. Note that deleting the hook_dispatch_cursor row restores the DEFAULT floor of 0 on next write (single id=1 row), which is the correct post-discard floor: the journal is empty, so everything in it is genuinely undispatched. Confirm that reading an absent row yields floor 0 rather than an error before choosing DELETE over UPDATE ... SET cursor = 0.

CAUTION worth checking: "a hook added later fires only on FUTURE events" is kept true by the floor advancing on every pass. After a discard the journal is empty, so a floor of 0 cannot replay history -- there is no history. Verify that a bootstrap/pull immediately after the discard does not then fire a hook backlog storm for the freshly pulled events; the 0.5.0-beta CHANGELOG records that fresh clones initialize the dispatch floor at the journal tail specifically to prevent that. A discard-then-pull may need the same floor seeding, which would make this UPDATE-to-tail rather than DELETE.

TEST. Mirror internal/store/sqlite/discard_local_inbox_tail_test.go (MTIX-66): journal events, advance the floor / write ledger rows, DiscardLocal, journal a new event, assert the dispatcher sees it. Red-first, and verify the red.

RELATED: relay_push_cursor is stranded by the same wipe but needs a ruling on pub_epoch before it can be fixed -- filed separately.
nodes.acceptance: After DiscardLocal, an event journaled next is visible to the hook dispatcher and fires matching hooks; hook_dispatch_cursor and hook_dispatch_ledger never reference a seq above the journal tail; a discard immediately followed by a pull does not fire a backlog storm for the pulled events. Regression test observed failing against the pre-fix code. make lint-go clean; internal/store/sqlite and internal/hooks suites green.
nodes.creator: cli

nodes.title: DiscardLocal strands relay_push_cursor above the wiped journal -- needs a pub_epoch ruling
nodes.prompt:
Found while fixing MTIX-66. Same wipe, same rowid-keyed-table defect class, but this one needs a RULING before it can be implemented -- do not fix it blind.

VERIFIED EMPIRICALLY. A probe seeded relay_push_cursor (id=1, cursor=8, pub_epoch=1, next_rs=5), ran DiscardLocal, and the row survived intact while the journal tail went to 0. Sibling finding: relay_ingest_cursor is correctly untouched -- it tracks per-peer REMOTE relay sequences, not local rowids, so a local wipe has no bearing on where this reader had reached in someone else's stream.

WHY IT BITES. relay_push_cursor.cursor is "the highest sync_events.rowid this peer has framed and appended to its own relay segment directory". sync_events has no AUTOINCREMENT, so after DiscardLocal the next insert takes rowid 1 again and the surviving cursor sits above the whole new journal. The publisher then frames NOTHING until the journal grows back past the old tail. The schema comment says the cursor advances only after the append returns so "a crash in between republishes rather than skips -- a skip would be a silent hole no reader could detect". A stale cursor produces exactly that undetectable hole, by construction, for every event written after a discard-local.

WHY IT IS NOT A ONE-LINE DELETE. The other stranded tables are pure position; this row also carries the publisher's IDENTITY IN THE FRAME (FR-21 5.7): pub_epoch and next_rs. Zeroing cursor alone would make the publisher re-emit relay sequence numbers it has ALREADY published under the same pub_epoch. Downstream readers key on (peer, epoch, rs); reusing an rs within an epoch means two different records claim the same coordinate. Deleting the whole row is worse -- it resets pub_epoch to the DEFAULT 1, which for a peer already past epoch 1 rewinds its identity and collides with its own history.

THE RULING NEEDED (Vimal). Which is correct for discard-local:
  (a) cursor = 0, pub_epoch = pub_epoch + 1, next_rs = 1 -- a discard is a new publishing incarnation, so take a fresh epoch. Readers see an epoch bump, which is the mechanism already built for exactly this "the publisher's history restarted" situation. Costs an epoch per discard.
  (b) cursor = 0, keep epoch and next_rs, let rs continue climbing -- no coordinate reuse because next_rs never rewinds, and no epoch churn. Needs confirmation that readers tolerate an rs gap/restart within an epoch and that nothing derives position from cursor alone.
  (c) leave relay_push_cursor alone and document that discard-local requires a relay re-bootstrap.
Recommendation is (a) if and only if epoch bumping is cheap for readers -- it is the only option that cannot produce a duplicate coordinate -- but this is FR-21 5.7 frame identity, which is exactly the "do not make this load-bearing without a ruling" category, and the answer depends on reader behaviour I have not traced. STOP AND ASK.

SCOPE NOTE. Whatever is chosen must land in the SAME transaction as the journal wipe in DiscardLocal, alongside the MTIX-66 inbox deletes and the MTIX-76 hook deletes, so a rollback cannot leave the journal and the publish position disagreeing.

TEST. Red-first regression: publish some events, DiscardLocal, journal new events, assert the publisher frames them and that no (epoch, rs) coordinate is reused across the discard.
nodes.acceptance: Ruling recorded on the ticket. After DiscardLocal, events journaled next are framed and appended by the publisher; no (pub_epoch, rs) coordinate is ever reused across a discard; the chosen behaviour lands in the same transaction as the journal wipe. Regression test observed failing against the pre-fix code.

nodes.title: QUALITY-STANDARDS.md 3.6 scenario list has drifted from the enforced traceability record
nodes.prompt:
QUALITY-STANDARDS.md 3.6 enumerates the safety-critical scenarios that MUST have dedicated coverage, numbered 1-19 inline. docs/traceability.json, which the same section names as the enforced mapping, now holds 28. Scenarios 20-27 (the FR-21 relay family) and 28 (local-state reset, MTIX-66/76/77) exist in the enforced record but not in the document that states the requirement.

WHY IT MATTERS rather than being cosmetic. 3.6 is the clause an auditor reads to learn what the project considers safety-critical; traceability.json is the machine-checked evidence that those scenarios have tests. When the prose list is a subset of the evidence, the document understates the project's own safety scope -- a reader auditing against 3.6 would conclude the relay transport carries no declared safety scenarios at all. Nothing is unguarded (the json is what CI enforces, and it is complete), so this is a documentation-integrity defect, not a coverage gap.

FIX. Bring 3.6's list into agreement with docs/traceability.json. Two options, pick one and state it in the document:
(a) enumerate all 28 inline, and add a check that the two stay in step -- otherwise this recurs on scenario 29;
(b) stop enumerating in prose, state the criteria for what qualifies as safety-critical, and point at traceability.json as the single normative list.
(b) is the stronger choice: one list, machine-enforced, cannot drift. 3.6 keeps the RULE and loses the inventory. If (b) is taken, keep a short illustrative sample in the prose so the section still communicates what the bar looks like.

Whichever is chosen, the drift itself should be made hard to repeat -- an enumeration maintained by hand next to a machine-checked list will drift again.

nodes.title: Relay publisher tail-verify attestation can outlive the journal it attested to
nodes.prompt:
Split from MTIX-77 by ruling. The cursor rewind shipped; this is the residual hazard, and it must be designed against QUALITY-STANDARDS.md (DO-178C, IEC 62304, NASA-STD-8739.8, MIL-STD-498, OWASP ASVS) rather than patched.

DESIGN PROPOSED, NOT YET APPROVED. Per the FR-21 house rule ("a spec change first, code second") and the 5.7 clause below, nothing is implemented until this design is ruled on.

== 1. HAZARD ==

FR-21 5.7 makes the startup tail-verify the detection half of publisher restore safety: before its first publish of a run, a publisher checks that the event ids in its newest segment's tail still exist in its journal, in order. Absent or out of order means the store was restored (or the relay tampered) and publishing halts with RELAY_PUBLISHER_DIVERGED.

The attestation that check produces is cached in a process-local bool (publisher.go: `verified`), documented as "run once per run". Nothing invalidates it. If the journal is replaced UNDER a live publisher, the publisher keeps publishing on the strength of an attestation about a journal that no longer exists.

MEASURED, not inferred. Probe: 5 events published (cursor seq 5), DiscardLocal, journal refilled to 8 rows.
- Fresh publisher process: n=0, diverged=true, correct loud refusal naming reset-peer.
- Publisher instance alive across the discard: n=3, diverged=false, no error. Pre-MTIX-77 it silently skipped rows 1-5. Post-MTIX-77 it no longer skips, but it still publishes a SECOND, UNRELATED history into the same segment stream under the SAME pub_epoch, with no operator ever told.

That defeats the purpose of pub_epoch. 5.7 exists so that post-restore events "carry fresh (pub_epoch, rs)" and the transition is explicit and auditable. An undeclared splice of two histories inside one epoch is the D-R9 outcome arriving through an innocent operation -- which is the exact sentence 5.7 opens with.

REACHABILITY: `mtix daemon` constructs one relay stack, hence one Publisher, for the process lifetime (tick/stack.go:124). An operator running `mtix sync discard-local` from a separate CLI while the daemon is up is the reachable path. This is the documented multi-process arrangement, not an exotic one.

== 2. WHY THE EXISTING CONTROL IS INSUFFICIENT ==

The control is sound; its VALIDITY WINDOW is unbounded. A monitor whose attestation can outlive the state it attested to is not a weaker monitor, it is a monitor that reports "verified" about something it never verified. This is the failure class the project already names: a gate that can silently no-op is worse than no gate, because it manufactures confidence.

5.7 anticipated an adjacent break and wrote the assumption down: "relay_push_cursor lives in the same store as the journal, so a restore rewinds cursor and journal together, atomically. If relay cursors ever move out of the store, this argument breaks and the semantics must be revisited." MTIX-77 restored that invariant for the cursor. The `verified` bool is the same assumption in a second place -- attestation state living OUTSIDE the store, in process memory, where nothing rewinds it with the journal. The spec's own reasoning applies verbatim and reaches the same conclusion.

== 3. PROPOSED DESIGN ==

NOT a durable "diverged" flag. Bound the attestation's validity instead, so the EXISTING mechanism stops being bypassable. No new verdict code, no new operator concept, no new terminal state, no change to the refusal or its recovery.

An attestation is valid only while the journal it was taken against is still the same journal. Two independent witnesses, both cheap:

(a) JOURNAL GENERATION (exact). A monotonic counter `meta.sync.journal_generation`, incremented in the SAME transaction as any reset of the journal's rowid space:
    INSERT INTO meta (key, value) VALUES ('meta.sync.journal_generation', '1')
    ON CONFLICT(key) DO UPDATE SET value = CAST(CAST(value AS INTEGER) + 1 AS TEXT)
  Self-seeding, monotonic, never reset -- a discard/restore/discard cycle can never return to an earlier generation. Absent row reads as 0. DiscardLocal is the ONLY production site that deletes from sync_events (verified by grep), so the maintenance burden is exactly one call site today.

(b) TAIL REGRESSION (needs no cooperation). The publisher records the journal tail its attestation was taken at. Ordinary operation only grows the tail; a tail BELOW the verified tail can only mean the rowid space was reset. One indexed MAX(rowid) per publish, a query the publish path already performs.

Publisher gains `verifiedGen` and `verifiedTail` beside `verified`. The cached attestation is honoured only while generation is unchanged AND tail has not regressed; otherwise verifyTail RE-RUNS. It does not refuse -- it re-establishes, and the existing 5.7 logic then decides.

Consequences, which are the point:
- Discard on a peer WITH published segments: re-verify finds published ids absent, diverges, refuses loudly, names reset-peer. Now true for a live daemon, not only a fresh process.
- Discard on a peer that never published: re-verify passes trivially, publishing continues. No spurious operator ticket -- which matters, because 5.7 warns that "operators trained to reflexively reset-peer are their own safety hazard".

WHY TWO WITNESSES. (a) alone relies on every future author of a journal-resetting operation remembering to bump it -- the same by-hand discipline that produced this defect family six times over. (b) alone has a narrow hole: a reset that regrows past the old tail before the publisher next runs. Neither hole is reachable through both. Defence in depth on a safety monitor, with the un-forgettable witness as the backstop for the exact one.

== 4. REJECTED: DURABLE "DIVERGED" FLAG ==

The obvious design -- DiscardLocal sets a persisted diverged flag the publisher reads -- is worse on three counts, and the comparison is the justification for the extra thought:
- It introduces a new TERMINAL persistent state with its own stuck-set failure mode: if the flag is set and reset-peer fails to clear it, publishing is bricked with no path back that does not involve hand-editing the database. The proposed design has no terminal state to get stuck; the worst false positive costs one extra verifyTail.
- It is a NOTIFICATION, not a witness. It works only if the writer remembers to send it. Every future journal-resetting operation must re-derive the same insight.
- It states a CONCLUSION ("you are diverged") where the truth is a PRECONDITION ("your attestation expired"). Those differ: a peer that never published is not diverged, and a flag would tell it that it was.

== 5. STANDARDS MAPPING (QUALITY-STANDARDS.md) ==

DO-178C 6.4 (verification) / 7 (configuration management): the design restores integrity of an existing verification monitor rather than adding a parallel one. Change control is the journal generation itself -- an auditable, monotonic record that the journal identity changed. 6.3 traceability: requirement (FR-21 5.7) -> design (this ticket + spec amendment) -> implementation -> named tests -> traceability.json.
IEC 62304 5.5.5 (change control) and ISO 14971 (risk): hazard, severity and mitigation stated in sections 1-3 above; the mitigation is verified by regression, not by inspection. Class C shape -- full traceability requirement -> design -> implementation -> test, independent verification mandatory (see section 8).
NASA-STD-8739.8: anomaly recorded with root cause and regression evidence; the safety-critical state transition (attestation valid -> void) is justified in the code at its site, per 5.3.4. IV&V: see section 8.
MIL-STD-498: this ticket plus the 5.7 amendment is the SDD content; the verification plan in section 7 is the STP content; completion comment will carry the STR content.
OWASP ASVS L2 V7 (error handling and logging): voiding an attestation is a security-relevant integrity event and MUST be logged at WARN naming the generation and tail transition -- a control that re-arms silently cannot be audited. V8 (data protection): the control protects integrity of a replicated data stream. Fail-secure: the DEFAULT on any doubt is to re-verify, never to assume validity; an unreadable generation MUST be treated as changed, not as unchanged.

== 6. FAILURE MODES ==

- Generation unreadable/corrupt -> treat as CHANGED, re-verify. Fail-secure. Never treat a read failure as "unchanged".
- Generation overflow -> int64 at one increment per discard-local; not reachable.
- Attestation voided spuriously (false positive) -> one extra verifyTail: a bounded segment tail scan plus one indexed lookup. Cost is negligible and the outcome is still correct.
- Publisher never re-verifies because it never publishes -> harmless: no publish, no hazard.
- RenameTo rewrites sync_events.node_id but does NOT delete rows: event ids and rowids are unchanged, so membership still holds. It MUST NOT bump the generation, and this is worth stating in the spec so a future author does not add it defensively and cause needless reset-peer tickets.
- Retention: nothing in production prunes sync_events today (verified). If that ever changes, tail-verify's membership check acquires a new false-positive path independent of this work -- flagged here so it is not discovered later.

== 7. VERIFICATION PLAN ==

Red-first, each observed failing, per QUALITY-STANDARDS 3.1. Coverage per 2.1 (service layer 95/90/100).
- Attestation survives ORDINARY journal growth (guards against re-verifying on every publish, which would silently make the cache pointless and mask a regression in the witness logic).
- Attestation voided by a generation change; the live-publisher discard path then diverges and refuses. This is the defect, pinned.
- Attestation voided by tail regression WITHOUT a generation change (simulate a future resetter that forgot to bump) -- pins the backstop independently, so it cannot rot unnoticed behind witness (a).
- A peer with no published segments is never falsely diverged after a discard.
- Unreadable generation is treated as changed (fail-secure).
Traceability: extend scenario 24 ("Relay Publisher Restore Never Silently Loses Post-Restore Work", FR-21 5.7, G1) with the new test names, in the same commit as the tests. Same safety property; this closes a hole in it rather than opening a new scenario.

== 8. INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION ==

NASA-STD-8739.8 and IEC 62304 Class C both require that the implementing agent not verify its own work. I found this defect, wrote the probe and am proposing the design; an independent review pass by a different agent is warranted before this is considered closed. Flagging rather than assuming.

== 9. RULINGS NEEDED ==

R1. Approve the approach: bounded attestation validity, NOT a durable diverged flag.
R2. Approve the new meta key name `meta.sync.journal_generation`. New persistent state, so it goes to you by the standing rule.
R3. Confirm the 5.7 spec amendment lands BEFORE the code, per the FR-21 rule. The amendment makes normative: an attestation is valid only for the journal generation and tail it was taken at; operations resetting the rowid space bump the generation in the same transaction; RenameTo explicitly does not.
R4. Confirm no new verdict code is wanted. The design deliberately reuses RELAY_PUBLISHER_DIVERGED, since the outcome genuinely is divergence -- only its detection becomes reliable.
nodes.acceptance: FR-21 5.7 amended before code. A publisher whose journal is reset beneath it re-establishes its attestation rather than trusting a stale one; a live daemon diverges and refuses exactly as a fresh process does; a peer that never published is never falsely diverged. Voiding is logged at WARN with the generation and tail transition. An unreadable generation is treated as changed. Regressions cover ordinary growth, generation change, tail regression without a generation change, the never-published case, and the fail-secure read; each observed failing first. Scenario 24 extended in the same commit as its tests. make lint-go clean; full suite green; independent review pass recorded.

nodes.title: Skip redundant auto-import via meta table export hash
nodes.description: Auto-import triggers on every command when tasks.json hash differs from stored hash. With multiple agents on the same machine, each mutation triggers an export (hash changes) which causes all other agents to do a full ImportModeReplace — a thundering herd problem. Fix: store last export hash in the meta table. If file hash matches last export hash, the file came from our own export — skip import. External changes (git pull) produce a different hash and import correctly.
nodes.prompt:
TDD approach — write failing test first.

TEST (in internal/service/sync_service_test.go):
TestAutoImport_SkipsWhenFileMatchesOwnExport: Create a sync service, insert nodes, call AutoExport (writes tasks.json + sets meta last_export_hash), then call AutoImport. Import should be skipped because the file hash matches the export hash. Verify by checking that nodes were NOT reimported (no write transaction occurred).

TestAutoImport_ImportsWhenFileChangedExternally: Create a sync service, insert nodes, call AutoExport, then modify tasks.json externally (simulate git pull), then call AutoImport. Import SHOULD trigger because file hash differs from export hash. Verify by checking the imported data matches the modified file.

TestAutoImport_ImportsWhenNoExportHashExists: Fresh database with no last_export_hash in meta. Place a tasks.json file. AutoImport should trigger (fail-safe to current behavior).

TestAutoImport_SkipsWhenSiblingAgentExported: Agent A exports (sets meta hash). Agent B has not exported. Agent B runs AutoImport. Should skip because meta hash matches file hash (Agent A and B share the same DB).

IMPLEMENTATION:
1. In AutoExport (sync_service.go), after writing tasks.json and hash files, write the file hash to meta: store.WriteDB().ExecContext(ctx, INSERT OR REPLACE INTO meta (key, value) VALUES ('last_export_hash', ?), fileHash)

2. In AutoImport (sync_service.go), after detecting file hash differs from stored hash, check meta: SELECT value FROM meta WHERE key = 'last_export_hash'. If file hash matches meta value, log at DEBUG level and return nil (skip import).

3. Fail-safe: if meta read fails or returns no row, proceed with import (current behavior).

Files: internal/service/sync_service.go, internal/service/sync_service_test.go
nodes.acceptance: 1. TestAutoImport_SkipsWhenFileMatchesOwnExport passes. 2. TestAutoImport_ImportsWhenFileChangedExternally passes. 3. TestAutoImport_ImportsWhenNoExportHashExists passes. 4. TestAutoImport_SkipsWhenSiblingAgentExported passes. 5. All existing tests pass. 6. Coverage >= 87%. 7. golangci-lint clean.

nodes.title: Wall-clock relay latency gate runs under -race on shared runners and fails on runner variance
nodes.prompt:
CI run 32734342738 failed on test-go (macos-latest) with:

  --- FAIL: TestRelayPublish_MeetsTheLatencyTarget
      "1.451752ms" is not less than or equal to "1ms"

This was NOT a code regression. Measured both sides on the same machine, -race, three runs each:
  pre-change  (8ca5703): 116.4, 118.2, 117.4 us/event  (mean ~117.3)
  post-change (d1e0f32): 118.2, 119.1, 116.8 us/event  (mean ~118.0)
Delta ~0.6%, inside run-to-run noise. The macOS runner measured 1451 us/event -- about 12x a healthy local machine -- so the runner was slow, not the code.

THE DEFECT is the gate's design, not the number.

1. It asserts WALL-CLOCK LATENCY inside the main test-go job, which runs with -race on shared GitHub runners. Wall-clock assertions on shared, unpinned, virtualised runners under a race detector measure the runner at least as much as the code. macos-latest in particular is a noisy-neighbour environment with no CPU guarantee.

2. The budget is admitted to be uncalibrated. The file's own CALIBRATION NOTE says relayPublishBudget is "a deliberately loose local-development ceiling, not the 9 number... Until that calibration runs, this guards against order-of-magnitude regressions only -- a publish path that quietly became 50x slower would still be caught, a 20% drift would not." Local headroom is only about 8.5x (117 us against a 1 ms ceiling), so a runner 9x slower than the developer's machine fails the build while the stated intent is to catch 50x regressions. The threshold does not implement the intent the note describes.

3. WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND ANNOYANCE. A gate that fails for reasons unrelated to the change under test teaches everyone to re-run it, and a gate people reflexively re-run is one that no longer gates. That is the same failure class this project has now fixed three times in a different guise (a control that is present but not effective) -- and here it degrades a real perf signal into noise. It also cost a false-positive investigation on an unrelated ticket.

OPTIONS, pick one:
(a) Move the wall-clock assertions out of the -race job into a dedicated perf job, no -race, and calibrate the constant on that rig. This is what MTIX-25 already specifies for the MTIX_PERF_LONG-gated tests ("NO -race"); this test is the same kind of assertion running in the wrong place, so the two should be decided together. MTIX-25 is the natural home and this may simply widen its scope.
(b) Keep it in the main job but make the ceiling honour the stated intent -- if it is meant to catch order-of-magnitude regressions, set it there (e.g. 10x measured local p50) so it cannot fire on runner variance.
(c) Gate it on a machine-class signal, skipping where no CPU guarantee exists. Least attractive: a check that skips on the platform where it most often fails is close to no check.

RECOMMENDATION: (a), folded into MTIX-25, with (b) applied to whatever remains in the main job so nothing wall-clock-sensitive runs under -race on a shared runner. Whatever is chosen, record the calibration basis next to the constant so the next person does not have to re-derive whether a failure is real.

DO NOT simply raise the number without recording why.
nodes.acceptance: The relay publish/ingest wall-clock assertions no longer fail a build because of CI runner variance: either moved to a dedicated perf job without -race and calibrated there, or given a ceiling that matches the order-of-magnitude intent stated in the calibration note. The basis for the chosen threshold is recorded beside the constant. Decided together with MTIX-25 rather than in isolation.

nodes.title: npm audit gate blocked: the MTIX-63 brace-expansion override pins a now-vulnerable version
nodes.prompt:
The release gate 'npm audit --audit-level=high' fails with 7 high advisories, blocking the v0.5.1-beta tag. Preflight step 5 (plain 'npm audit', stricter) also fails.

Root cause: MTIX-63 (commit b94d0f1, the v0.5.0-beta release commit) added a HARD PIN override in web/package.json:
    "overrides": { "brace-expansion": "5.0.8" }
to clear two advisories at the time. A newer advisory (brace-expansion DoS, bypassing the CVE-2026-14257 mitigation) covers the range 4.0.0 - 5.0.8, so the pinned version is now itself vulnerable. Because the override hard-pins an exact version, 'npm audit fix' cannot reach the patched 5.0.9 — the pin blocks its own remedy. The vulnerable copies cascade: brace-expansion -> minimatch -> @eslint/config-array, @eslint/eslintrc, eslint.

Not introduced by MTIX-81: web/package.json and web/package-lock.json are byte-identical between v0.5.0-beta and the v0.5.1-beta candidate. This is advisory drift since 2026-07-28.

Blast radius: all affected packages are devDependencies (eslint toolchain, js-yaml, nanoid, postcss-selector-parser). Runtime deps are only react and react-dom; 'npm audit --omit=dev' reports 0. Nothing vulnerable ships inside the binary. The gate still blocks the release because CI does not pass --omit=dev.

Investigated remedies:
  - 'npm audit fix' (non-force): 8 -> 5 high, then stalls on the override.
  - Fresh lockfile re-resolve: 8 -> 5 high, same wall.
  - Removing the override entirely: 0 vulnerabilities; brace-expansion resolves naturally to the patched 5.0.9. The upstream eslint tree has caught up, so the pin is obsolete.
  - No semver-major bump is needed; every advisory reports fixAvailable=true. eslint stays on 9.x.

Local note: npm 11.2.0 crashes with 'Cannot read properties of null (reading edgesOut)' on install/update in this tree; npm 11.19.1 works.
nodes.acceptance:
1. 'npm audit --audit-level=high' exits 0 (CI release gate).
2. Plain 'npm audit' reports 0 vulnerabilities (preflight step 5, stricter).
3. No semver-major dependency bumps; eslint remains 9.x and runtime deps (react, react-dom) unchanged.
4. Lint, typecheck, build, and the 267 web tests all still pass.
5. The rebuilt SPA bundle is verified equivalent to the previous one (minifier identifier renaming only, no semantic change), and internal/web/dist is regenerated to match so 'make embed-check' stays green.
6. The obsolete hard pin is removed rather than re-pinned to a new exact version, so future patch releases flow in without another stale-pin cycle.

    FAIL github.com/hyper-swe/mtix/internal/store/sqlite  600.061s

Not a functional failure and not a hang. The named test had just started (0s); the package as a whole reached Go's default 10-minute per-binary timeout. The goroutine dump shows the work in progress was an ordinary fsync through modernc sqlite (_unixSync -> Xfsync -> syscall), i.e. the runner was simply slow, not deadlocked.

Root cause is a workflow asymmetry. MTIX-72 (commit 0460cde) added an explicit timeout to the race invocation, but only in ci.yml:
    ci.yml:40       go test ./... -race -count=1 -timeout 20m
    release.yml:68  go test ./... -race -count=1 -p 1          <-- no -timeout, so the default 10m applies
release.yml:72 (the coverage invocation, same package set, also -p 1) likewise has no -timeout.

This is the same shape as MTIX-81: a fix applied in one place and not the parallel one, so the release path kept the weaker behaviour while CI looked green.

Evidence it is variance against a too-tight limit rather than a regression: the immediately preceding run (33536607605) on a byte-identical Go tree passed the same step in 12m47s total for ALL packages. This run, internal/store/sqlite alone consumed 600s before being killed. Roughly a 2x slower runner turned a pass into a fail. Note also -p 1 serializes packages, so the wall clock is the sum, but -timeout applies per test binary, so the limit that matters is the single slowest package.

Neither release attempt for v0.5.1-beta has yet reached test-go-postgres-cloud, so the Neon/Supabase cloud contract gate remains unverified for this tree.
nodes.acceptance:
1. release.yml's race invocation carries an explicit -timeout matching ci.yml (20m), and the coverage invocation carries one too.
2. A release run reaches and passes the race and coverage steps without a timeout panic.
3. The two workflows' shared test invocations are consistent, so a timeout change in one cannot silently leave the other behind — ideally checked or factored rather than duplicated by hand.
4. No test logic changes: this is a CI limit fix, not a fix for slow tests. If internal/store/sqlite genuinely needs ~10m under -race, size the budget from measured data and record it.
nodes.creator: cli

nodes.title: cloud-gate canary claims to verify connectivity but never connects — passed while every test failed to connect
nodes.prompt:
In release run 33542273579 the cloud gate's canary step reported PASS on both providers, and then every test in the transport suite immediately failed to connect. The canary is a false green.

The step is named 'Canary — DSN actually connects (guards against a silent skip)' and its inline comment states it 'PASSES only on a real connection'. Both claims are false. It runs TestSource_AcceptsTestDSNViaEnv, which is:

    dsn := requireTestDSN(t)
    dir := withMTIXDir(t)
    t.Setenv(transport.EnvDSN, dsn)
    got, err := transport.Source(dir)
    require.NoError(t, err)
    require.Equal(t, dsn, got)

It asserts only that Source() echoes back the DSN string it was handed. It performs no I/O and opens no connection, so it passes whenever the secret is merely PRESENT — regardless of whether the database is reachable, awake, or still exists.

MTIX-42 added this canary to stop the gate reporting a false green when a secret was missing. It does cover that case. It does not cover an unreachable or deleted database, which is the failure that actually occurred:
  supabase: FATAL (ENOTFOUND) tenant/user postgres.<redacted> not found (SQLSTATE XX000) via aws-1-us-west-2.pooler.supabase.com
  neon:     connection refused, after a 10s timeout

This is the third instance in one release cycle of a check that cannot fail the way its name promises — see MTIX-81 (the preflight embed gate that a preceding build silently repaired) and MTIX-85 (a timeout raised in ci.yml but not release.yml). Same class: the gate's label asserts more than its implementation checks.

Fix direction: the canary must open a real connection and round-trip something trivial (SELECT 1, or a Ping through the same transport path the suite uses, via the pooler host the suite actually targets — the direct-port DSN would not have caught this either). Keep failing closed on an unset secret.
nodes.acceptance:
1. The canary opens a real connection to the same endpoint the suite uses and fails when the database is unreachable, suspended, or deleted.
2. Verified red: with a DSN pointing at a valid-format but unreachable endpoint, the canary FAILS. It must not pass merely because the secret is set.
3. Still fails closed when the secret is unset or empty (the MTIX-42 behaviour is preserved, not replaced).
4. The step name and its inline comment describe exactly what is asserted, so the label cannot outrun the implementation again.
5. Consider auditing the other gates for the same pattern: a named check whose implementation cannot fail the way the name implies.
nodes.creator: cli

nodes.title: DSN rejects passwords containing / ? # % or space; users must percent-encode by hand
nodes.prompt:
A user connecting mtix to an AWS RDS sync hub had to percent-encode their database password by hand before mtix would accept the DSN:

    export ENC_PGPASSWORD=$(python3 -c "import urllib.parse,sys; print(urllib.parse.quote(sys.argv[1], safe=''))" "$PGPASSWORD")
    export MTIX_SYNC_DSN="postgres://mtixhub:${ENC_PGPASSWORD}@${RDSHOST}:5432/postgres?sslmode=verify-full&sslrootcert=..."

That extra step should not be necessary. The password came from AWS Secrets Manager, which generates characters that break URI parsing.

Root cause: internal/store/postgres/transport/dsn.go parseDSN() accepts only the postgres:// URL form and hands it to Go's net/url.Parse. Measured behaviour of url.Parse on postgres://user:<pw>@host:5432/db:

    @      OK    (Go splits userinfo on the LAST @)
    :      OK
    /      FAIL  invalid port ":p" after host
    ?      FAIL  invalid port ":p" after host
    #      FAIL  invalid port ":p" after host
    %      FAIL  invalid URL escape "%ss"
    space  FAIL  net/url: invalid userinfo

So @ and : already work — the reported break is /, ?, #, % or space. Note % is especially common in generated passwords, and its failure message (invalid URL escape) gives the user no hint that encoding is the fix.

Second defect in the same function: its doc comment claims a fallback that does not exist —
    // parseDSN parses a postgres:// or postgresql:// URL form. Falls back
    // to wrapping a key=value form into URL form so url.Parse can handle
    // it; rejects anything else.
The body has no key=value branch at all; it returns an error for anything not prefixed postgres://. There is no test covering key=value input. This is the same label-outruns-implementation pattern as MTIX-81, MTIX-85 and MTIX-86.

Why this is NOT a trivial patch, and was deliberately kept out of v0.5.1-beta:
  - The only caller is EnforceTLSPosture (dsn.go:167), the single choke point that enforces sslmode=verify-full, performs the loopback check for weak TLS, injects sslrootcert from MTIX_SYNC_SSLROOTCERT, and re-serialises via parsed.String(). Changing the parser changes how TLS posture is enforced, so it is security-relevant, not cosmetic.
  - Percent-encoding heuristics on the URL form are genuinely ambiguous: in postgres://u:p/ss@host/db it is undecidable whether the password is p or p/ss. Do not guess.
  - v0.5.1-beta deliberately contains ZERO Go changes, which is what lets its coverage and cloud-Postgres gate results carry over unchanged from v0.5.0-beta. Adding Go there would have invalidated that argument mid-release.

Preferred design: accept the libpq key=value form (host=... user=... password=... sslmode=...), which has no escaping ambiguity and needs no encoding for any character. pgx already parses both forms natively — pool.go:102 calls pgxpool.ParseConfig, which accepts key=value today. The work is to stop routing TLS posture through net/url: parse with pgx.ParseConfig, read and set sslmode/sslrootcert and read the host off the resulting *pgx.ConnConfig, and return something pgxpool can consume, rather than doing string surgery on a URL.

Also worth adding as a zero-ambiguity escape hatch: an MTIX_SYNC_PASSWORD env var supplying the password out-of-band. That is the same shape MTIX-61 already adopted for backup, which hands pg_dump PG* environment variables precisely to dodge URI parsing.

Whatever lands, the error message for a genuinely unparseable DSN must say that a special character in the password needs encoding, or point at the key=value form. Today it surfaces a raw net/url error.
nodes.acceptance:
1. A DSN whose password contains / ? # % space @ : is accepted without manual percent-encoding, via the libpq key=value form at minimum.
2. Table-driven tests cover each of those characters in both the URL form and the key=value form, asserting the password reaches pgx intact — the password recovered from the parsed config must equal the input byte-for-byte.
3. TLS posture is unchanged and still enforced for every accepted form: sslmode defaults to verify-full, weak sslmode still requires --insecure-tls AND a loopback host, and sslrootcert injection still works. Existing EnforceTLSPosture tests pass untouched.
4. The parseDSN doc comment matches the implementation — either implement the key=value fallback it describes or delete the claim. A test covers whichever is true.
5. An unparseable DSN produces an actionable error naming the likely cause (special character in the password) instead of a raw net/url message; the error never leaks the credential.
6. Redaction still holds: RedactDSN handles every newly accepted form, verified by test.
7. Not shipped in v0.5.1-beta. Lands in its own release with a full gate run, including the cloud-Postgres contract gate against a real hub.
nodes.creator: cli

nodes.title: sync backfill orders synthesized create_node events by created_at, not topologically — clone hits FOREIGN KEY on reparented children
nodes.prompt:
Reported against 0.5.1-beta: 'mtix sync backfill' synthesizes create_node events in created_at order rather than topologically, so any consumer applying in lamport order (e.g. mtix sync clone) hits FOREIGN KEY constraint failed on the child — deterministically. Reporter saw 8 violations across the SQP-6 and SQP-7 subtrees, e.g. SQP-7.1 at lamport 233 under parent SQP-7 at lamport 1818.

CONFIRMED and root-caused.

internal/store/sqlite/sync_backfill.go collectBackfillNodes() walked the table with

    ORDER BY created_at ASC, id ASC

and runBackfillInTx assigns lamport monotonically in walk order. created_at is wall-clock and carries no topological meaning: reparenting and renumbering leave a child row whose created_at predates the parent it now hangs under (see assignParentToFormerRoots in sync_reconcile.go:344, the --import-as path, which sets parent_id on existing former roots). Such a child gets a LOWER lamport than its parent.

The consequence chain is fully verified:
  - schema.go:95   FOREIGN KEY (parent_id) REFERENCES nodes(id)
  - store.go:213   PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON on all connections
  - inserting a child before its parent under that FK => 'FOREIGN KEY constraint failed'

Reproduced on the released 0.5.1-beta binary: create child, wait, create parent, reparent child under it, run backfill -> child emitted at lamport 3, parent at lamport 4, 1 topological violation. Replaying the emitted stream in lamport order into a fresh FK-enforced schema fails exactly as reported.

Note the pre-existing doc comment on Backfill asserted 'Lamport is monotonic in walk order (correct per the sync invariants — lamport is causal, not wall-clock)' while the walk order was in fact wall-clock, so the comment claimed a causality the ordering did not provide. Corrected as part of the fix.

Adjacent hole spotted, NOT fixed here: verifyNodesInvariants checks the parent row EXISTS but does not filter it by deleted_at, while collectBackfillNodes excludes deleted rows. A live child under a soft-deleted parent therefore passes the invariant check yet has no parent in the emitted set. The new ordering treats that child as a root so backfill still succeeds, but a consumer would have nothing to attach it to. Worth its own ticket.
nodes.acceptance:
1. Backfill emits a parent before its children regardless of created_at. DONE.
2. Ordering is STABLE: a stream that was already topological comes back in the same created_at order, so the fix does not churn correct event streams. DONE — a plain BFS was rejected for exactly this reason after the preservation test caught it.
3. Regression tests proven red against the unfixed code, then green. DONE — TestBackfill_EmitsParentBeforeReparentedChild and TestBackfill_TopologicalAcrossDeepSubtree both fail without the fix; TestBackfill_PreservesCreatedAtOrderWhenAlreadyTopological guards the stability property.
4. A child whose parent is absent from the set (soft-deleted parent) is treated as a root rather than dropped or erroring. DONE.
5. No event is ever lost, including on a hypothetical parent_id cycle: unemitted rows are appended rather than dropped. DONE.
6. Full Go suite, go vet and golangci-lint clean. DONE.
7. Ship in the next release with a changelog entry; needs a full gate run since this is a Go change.
nodes.creator: cli

nodes.title: no supported way to regenerate a backfill stream: --force appends, --discard-local destroys nodes
nodes.prompt:
Fixing MTIX-88 exposed that there is no supported, non-destructive way to regenerate a backfill stream. A user who backfilled on 0.5.1-beta or earlier has a badly-ordered stream and no safe command to replace it.

Measured behaviour of the two candidates:

1. 'mtix sync backfill --force' APPENDS, it does not regenerate. Verified: a project with 2 create_node events had 4 after --force, and the original 2 event_ids were still present. Replaying the combined stream in lamport order still fails on the FOREIGN KEY, because the old badly-ordered events survive ahead of the new correct ones:
     after 0.5.1 backfill:  SQP-1(l3) -> SQP-2(l4)
     after 0.5.2 --force:   SQP-1(l3) -> SQP-2(l4) -> SQP-2(l5) -> SQP-1(l6)   <- still violates
   Worse, push dedupes on event_id with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and --force mints FRESH ids, so the duplicates are accepted by the hub rather than deduped. sync_backfill.go:34 already warns about exactly this, so the behaviour is known — it is the absence of an alternative that is the gap.

2. 'mtix sync reconcile --discard-local' is destructive to the canonical data. The help says 'drop local nodes/events and take hub state' and that is accurate: DELETE FROM nodes at sync_reconcile.go:143. Verified: after --discard-local the journal was empty AND all nodes were gone. It also adopts hub state, which is precisely wrong when the hub is what holds the bad stream. Note sync_backfill.go:34 currently POINTS AT this command as the way to 're-backfill from scratch', which will cost someone their local data.

The only working procedure today is raw SQL: back up, DELETE FROM sync_events against .mtix/data/mtix.db, then 'mtix sync backfill'. Verified end to end — clean topological stream, nodes preserved, no duplicates. That is not something to put in release notes.

There is also no hub-side purge. If the bad stream was pushed, those rows must be deleted from the hub's sync_events directly or both orderings coexist and the clone keeps failing. 'mtix sync relay reset-peer' is unrelated.

This is the same class as MTIX-86 and MTIX-81: the documented remedy does not do what its description implies.
nodes.acceptance:
1. A supported command regenerates a project's local sync journal WITHOUT touching the nodes table — e.g. 'mtix sync backfill --regenerate', or --force changed to wipe-then-emit rather than append. It must not run DELETE FROM nodes, and must not be gated by the MTIX-90 typed confirmation unless it also destroys tickets (it should not).
2. If --force keeps append semantics, it refuses with an actionable message when sync_events is non-empty and points at the regenerate path, instead of silently doubling the history.
3. (DONE under MTIX-90) The guidance in sync_backfill.go no longer sends operators to 'reconcile --discard-local'. No doc, error message or release note may point at an irreversible command as a routine remedy.
4. (REMOVED — superseded by MTIX-92) No hub-side reset. The multi-prefix DELETE FROM sync_events on a shared hub is out of scope and must not be built: after 'mtix sync repair-uids' a regenerated stream re-pushes as a same-logical-node no-op, so remediation is local regenerate + (once, for hubs pushed by a pre-MTIX-91 client) the uid repair. Any future proposal for a hub-side delete must obey docs/DESTRUCTIVE-COMMANDS.md.
5. (RE-SCOPED) Ordering is still enforced, but locally: regenerating marks the fresh events 'pending', so nothing depends on a hub cleanup step. The regenerate command must document that events it emits carry the node's existing uid (emitUIDFor), which is what makes the re-push a no-op.
6. (DONE under MTIX-91) Push reports a diagnosable error when a regenerated create collides with an already-registered node.
7. 'mtix sync init <dsn>' either persists the DSN or says plainly that MTIX_SYNC_DSN must be set for subsequent commands; 'sync clone' documents that the target must be 'mtix init'-ed first.
8. An e2e regression test covers the whole loop against a real Postgres hub — bad stream pushed, local regenerate, (uid repair when the hub was pushed by an old client), push, clone — asserting the clone applies with no FK error and the reparented hierarchy is intact. e2e/sync_uid_repair_test.go already covers the repair half; the regenerate command's test extends it. It must FAIL against today's behaviour (no regenerate command exists).
9. Any destructive step obeys MTIX-90's confirmation rule (docs/DESTRUCTIVE-COMMANDS.md). Given criterion 4, there should be none.

nodes.title: bulk-delete and irreversible commands need an unbypassable confirmation; --discard-local can silently destroy a deployment
nodes.prompt:
Product requirement from the founder, prompted by the MTIX-88/89 investigation: an irreversible command that wipes tickets can get mtix thrown out of a deployment. Losing a team's ticket history once is unrecoverable trust damage. No flag may be able to skip the warning.

Concrete danger found while investigating MTIX-89:
  'mtix sync reconcile --discard-local --yes' runs DELETE FROM nodes (sync_reconcile.go:143) plus DELETE FROM sync_events, sync_conflicts, applied_events and the inbox/hook bookkeeping. It destroys the local canonical data and adopts hub state. Verified on a throwaway store: after the command, nodes = 0.
  Today --yes alone is enough. There is no typed confirmation, no snapshot, no warning naming how many tickets are about to be destroyed.
  Worse, sync_backfill.go:34 actively RECOMMENDS this command as the way to 're-backfill from scratch'. An operator following our own error text to fix an ordering bug would lose every local ticket. That is the exact scenario this ticket exists to prevent.

Also note the CLI help for reconcile says 'drop local nodes/events and take hub state'. That is accurate, but it reads like journal maintenance rather than 'this deletes every ticket in this store'. The wording does not carry the weight of the operation.

Requirement: any command that bulk-deletes tickets, or is otherwise irreversible, must show a warning that states plainly what will be destroyed and how many rows, and must require a confirmation that CANNOT be satisfied by a flag. --yes / --force must not bypass it.

Design tension to resolve deliberately, not by accident: mtix is agent-native and runs in CI and in automation. A prompt that no flag can satisfy makes these commands unusable non-interactively — which is arguably correct for 'delete every ticket', but it must be a decided position, not a regression. Suggested shape, following the kubectl/terraform precedent: require the operator to TYPE a value that proves intent and cannot be guessed by a script author on autopilot — e.g. the project prefix, or the exact node count. A flag cannot supply it; a human at a terminal can. When stdin is not a TTY the command REFUSES with instructions rather than proceeding, so automation fails closed instead of silently wiping a store. cmd/mtix/create.go already has the interactive-confirm precedent (confirmNewProject, reading from createInput), so the plumbing exists.

Commands to audit, not only reconcile: anything reaching DELETE FROM nodes, bulk status transitions, 'mtix sync migrate --yes', GC/prune paths, and any future hub-side reset from MTIX-89 (which deletes rows on a SHARED hub, so it is even less forgiving).
nodes.acceptance:
1. Every command that bulk-deletes tickets or is otherwise irreversible requires a typed confirmation that no flag can satisfy. --yes and --force explicitly do NOT bypass it.
2. The warning names the operation, the exact scope (project prefix / hub), and the COUNT of tickets and events to be destroyed, before the prompt.
3. Non-TTY stdin makes the command REFUSE with instructions, never proceed. Automation fails closed. Covered by a test that pipes stdin.
4. An inventory of affected commands exists and each is either gated or explicitly documented as safe, so the audit is not silently partial.
5. No error message, doc, help text or release note recommends an irreversible command as a routine remedy. Specifically: sync_backfill.go:34 stops pointing at --discard-local.
6. The reconcile help text states plainly that --discard-local deletes every ticket in the local store, rather than the softer 'drop local nodes/events'.
7. Consider taking an automatic snapshot ('mtix backup') before any destructive path, so a mistake is recoverable rather than terminal. Decide and record the position either way.
8. Tests: a piped-stdin run refuses; a wrong typed value aborts with no mutation; the correct value proceeds. Verified red against today's behaviour, where --yes alone wipes the store.
nodes.creator: cli

nodes.title: sync push never sends uid to the hub, so the same-logical-node no-op can never fire
nodes.prompt:
Found while answering whether MTIX-89's remediation depends on nodes.uid being populated. It does not — the uid is populated and correctly carried on the local event. The client simply never SENDS it.

cmd/mtix/sync_push.go:183 reads the pending queue with:
    SELECT event_id, project_prefix, node_id, op_type, payload,
           wall_clock_ts, lamport_clock, vector_clock,
           author_id, author_machine_hash
    FROM sync_events WHERE sync_status = 'pending'
There is no uid column in that projection, so every pushed event reaches the hub with uid unset. Verified against a real Postgres hub: after a normal 'mtix sync push', every row on the hub had uid = NULL, while the corresponding local sync_events rows carried the correct node uid.

internal/store/sqlite/sync_divergence.go:240 has the same projection and the same omission.

Consequence — this defeats the MTIX-30.15 false-collision fix entirely. lookupRegisteredCreate (registry.go:82) resolves a registered row's EFFECTIVE uid as 'its stored uid, or its event_id when uid is NULL'. Because the stored uid is always NULL, the effective uid is always the event_id. So when a re-emitted create arrives carrying the node's real uid, it can never match the registered effective uid, registryDecide takes the DISTINCT-node branch, and the hub demands a renumber. The 'same logical node -> noop' case documented at registry.go:138 is unreachable for any pushed create.

That is the actual mechanism behind the MTIX-89 collision, and it is NOT fixed by migrating old deployments: the uid exists locally on every current store, it is just dropped in transit.

Reproduced end to end on a throwaway Neon branch:
  local nodes:   U-2 uid=01a0628b-c68d-...
  local event:   event_id=01a0628c-93b4-792f-...  uid=01a0628b-c68d-...   (correct)
  hub row:       event_id=01a0628b-c6fc-748c-...  uid=<NULL>              (uid lost)
  re-push:       error: resolve renumber for 01a0628c-93b4-792f-...:
                        settle uid 01a0628c-93b4-792f-...: not found
Note the identifier in that error is an EVENT_ID, not a uid, so the message is doubly misleading — it sent this investigation down the wrong path twice.

Why our tests missed it: the e2e helper readPendingForTest (e2e/sync_e2e_test.go:371) DOES select uid. The harness is more correct than production, so e2e exercises a code path the CLI never takes. My own new test in e2e/sync_backfill_reparent_test.go passed for exactly this reason while the CLI failed on identical input. Any fix must close that divergence or the harness will keep hiding regressions.
nodes.acceptance:
1. The push projection in cmd/mtix/sync_push.go includes uid, and the value reaches the hub. Verified by asserting a non-NULL uid on the hub row after a push.
2. The same omission in internal/store/sqlite/sync_divergence.go:240 is fixed, or documented as deliberate with a reason.
3. Re-pushing a re-emitted create for an existing node is a NO-OP, not a renumber: registryDecide's same-uid branch is reachable and covered by a test at the transport layer.
4. The e2e harness stops diverging from production — readPendingForTest either calls the production reader or the projection is shared, so a missing column cannot pass e2e again.
5. 'settle uid <id>: not found' names the right identifier and says what actually happened (this node is already registered on the hub under a different event id).
6. Regression test proven red against current behaviour: today the hub stores uid NULL and the re-push renumbers.
7. Re-evaluate MTIX-89 after this lands. If a re-push becomes a clean no-op, the multi-prefix hub reset may be unnecessary and MTIX-89 shrinks to a local regenerate path.
8. Assess whether existing hubs need a backfill of the uid column, since every event pushed to date has uid NULL.
nodes.creator: cli

nodes.title: hub uid repair: stamp existing hub create rows with their node uid so re-push no-ops instead of colliding
nodes.prompt:
Follow-up to MTIX-91. That fix makes the CLIENT send uid, but every event pushed by any release to date sits on the hub with uid NULL. The hub resolves a registered create's effective uid as 'stored uid, or event_id when NULL' (transport/registry.go), so a fixed client sending the correct uid still mismatches against those old rows and the collision persists. Verified: nulling the uid column on a hub and re-pushing with the fixed binary reproduces the failure identically.

So every existing deployment needs a one-time repair before regenerate + re-push works.

The repair is non-destructive and already prototyped end to end. For each local node with a uid, stamp the hub's create row where the uid is still NULL, matched on (project_prefix, node_id):

    UPDATE sync_events SET uid = $1
     WHERE project_prefix = $2 AND node_id = $3
       AND op_type = 'create_node' AND uid IS NULL

Nothing is deleted and no populated uid is overwritten. After running it against a hub whose rows had been nulled, the same re-push that had just failed reported '2 accepted, 0 renumbered, 0 conflicts'.

This matters beyond convenience: it lets MTIX-89 drop its multi-prefix DELETE-based hub reset. Regenerate + re-push becomes a clean no-op, so remediation is a local regenerate plus this repair — no destructive operation on a shared hub at all. That directly serves MTIX-90, which wants irreversible bulk deletes gated or eliminated.

Design notes: the client is the only party that knows the mapping, since the hub never received the uid, so this has to run from a CLI with the local store. It is idempotent (the uid IS NULL guard). Scope it per project prefix and report a count. Consider whether it belongs under 'mtix sync doctor' as a repair action rather than a standalone destructive-sounding command.
nodes.acceptance:
1. A supported command performs the repair from a client that holds the local store, idempotently, scoped by project prefix, reporting how many hub rows it stamped.
2. It never deletes a row and never overwrites a non-NULL uid.
3. A dry-run reports what WOULD be stamped without mutating.
4. After the repair, regenerate + re-push against a previously-pushed project is a no-op: 0 renumbered, 0 conflicts. Covered by an e2e test against a real Postgres hub, proven red before the repair runs.
5. Nodes present on the hub but absent locally are reported rather than silently skipped, so a partial repair is visible.
6. Documented as the upgrade step for anyone who pushed with a pre-MTIX-91 client, with the reason stated plainly.
7. MTIX-89 re-scoped once this lands: if remediation no longer needs a hub reset, remove that from its acceptance criteria rather than leaving a destructive path specified.
nodes.creator: cli

nodes.title: mtix sync doctor advertises 5 health checks but now runs up to 13
nodes.prompt:
The relay checks added in MTIX-64.8 were wired into runSyncDoctor without updating the count the command advertises. Four places still say five:

  cmd/mtix/sync_doctor.go:29   // DoctorReport aggregates the 5 health checks per FR-18 / MTIX-15.7.3.
  cmd/mtix/sync_doctor.go:48   Long: 'Run 5 health checks against the local store and the BYO Postgres hub:'
  USERMANUAL.md:1694           'mtix sync doctor  # 5 health checks: PG reachable, schema current, ...'
  docs/CLI_REFERENCE.md:1338   (regenerated FROM the stale Long string, so it inherits the error)

Actual behaviour: 5 hub checks, plus 1 row when no relay is configured ('relay configured' — not configured is not unhealthy), or 8 relay rows when one is (reachable, record, key, publishing, peers, poll cadence, snapshots, privacy). So the real count is 6 or 13, never 5.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A NUMBER: the Long string is what 'mtix sync doctor --help' prints, and it enumerates the five hub checks by name. A user reading it has no idea the relay is examined at all, so a relay row that fails arrives unexplained — and the docs give them nothing to look up. It also quietly undercuts the exit-2 contract: someone auditing 'what does doctor actually gate on' gets an answer that is wrong by more than half.

I INTRODUCED THIS in MTIX-64.8 and did not notice; found later by grepping for stale doc claims. Note CLI_REFERENCE.md is AutoGenerated from the cobra help, so fixing sync_doctor.go and regenerating is what corrects it — editing CLI_REFERENCE directly would be undone on the next 'mtix docs generate'.

FIX: make the help text describe both families without hardcoding a total that will rot again — the count changes with configuration, so naming the groups ('hub checks' and 'relay checks, when a relay is configured') is more durable than any number.
nodes.acceptance: mtix sync doctor --help describes the relay checks as well as the hub ones and states no count that a configuration change can falsify. USERMANUAL matches. CLI_REFERENCE is regenerated rather than hand-edited. A test pins that the help text does not claim a fixed number of checks.

nodes.title: CHANGELOG has no entry for the FR-21 file relay transport
nodes.prompt:
The FR-21 file relay (epic MTIX-64) shipped every build deliverable across MTIX-64.2 through 64.8 — nine packages under internal/relay, a nine-verb 'mtix sync relay' command group, a daemon phase, seven sync.relay.* config keys, doctor checks, and four public documentation edits. CHANGELOG.md contains zero occurrences of 'FR-21' or 'relay'.

WHY THIS IS NOT COSMETIC: the changelog is how a user discovers that a second sync transport exists at all. Someone on a machine that cannot reach Postgres — the exact audience this was built for — has no way to learn it is now possible. It is also the artifact a release is assembled from, so an unreleased epic with no entry is how a whole feature ships silently or, worse, gets left out of the release notes entirely and is presumed unshipped.

The last tag is v0.5.0-beta; FR-21 is unreleased, so this needs writing before the next tag rather than after.

CONTENT WORTH CARRYING (all public-safe, FR-21 by number only, no internal file references — the sanitization needles apply):
- what it is: the same events carried through a shared directory instead of a database connection, for peers that cannot open one
- the three motivating shapes, generically: a sandboxed runtime that shares a folder but has no network; an isolated network permitting controlled file movement but not a reachable database; a small team unwilling to provision Postgres
- that a peer may hold both transports and becomes a gateway between them at no cost
- that a peer needing no daemon is first-class ('mtix sync relay tick')
- the honest limits, which the security model already states and the changelog should not soften: the shared key authenticates the fleet rather than the individual peer; records are authenticated but NOT encrypted; deletion of relay files is loud and recoverable but not prevented
- the new command group and the sync.relay.* configuration keys

Cross-check the wording against docs/SECURITY-MODEL.md's relay section and the USERMANUAL topology section so the three do not drift apart on first read.
nodes.acceptance: CHANGELOG.md carries an FR-21 entry in the unreleased section, naming the transport, the command group, the config keys, and the three honest limits. Wording is public-safe and consistent with SECURITY-MODEL and USERMANUAL. Reviewed before the next tag is cut.

nodes.title: Sync containment hotfix v0.5.4-beta: own-event replay, push wedge, pull gaps, hub privileges, agent guidance
nodes.description:
A field report showed `mtix sync pull` re-applying events the same client had already pushed. Investigation (maintainer design record ADR-006) found a family of sync defects: pull replays the client's own events (spurious conflicts, and status/claim events that revert newer local status); push can stop draining its queue forever after a lost acknowledgement; pull can permanently miss events (Lamport ties at page boundaries, and late pushes stamped below a peer's cursor); hub table privileges need hardening; and agents have no accurate, provider-neutral sync guidance.

The complete fix is the ADR-006 replication-core redesign (protocol 2, later epics). This epic is ADR-006 phase 0: the minimal, client-side containment that stops ongoing damage in 0.5.x installations without a protocol change, heals damage already done, hardens hub privileges, and ships the 0.5.x edition of the agent sync instruction set.
nodes.prompt:
Originating ask (maintainer, 2026-09-23): investigate a customer sync bug, reject point fixes proposed without source access, design a robust and recoverable sync, and first ship a containment release for 0.5.x users. Priority order: hub privilege hardening (.1) first, then replay (.2), push wedge (.3), late-event sweep (.5), page-boundary skip (.4), status repair (.6), honesty fixes (.7), agent instruction set (.8), release (.9).

Common rules for every child of this epic:
- Read the dev directives (CLAUDE.md, imported from ../mtix-dev/CLAUDE.md) first. TDD red-first: commit each regression test failing against the old code and say so in the commit message.
- Patch lineage: branch fix/MTIX-<id>/<desc> off release/0.5.x (cut from the v0.5.0-beta tag; main carries unreleased FR-21 relay work). Merge back into release/0.5.x, then merge release/0.5.x into main. Children that touch relay code (main only) branch from main.
- Compatibility: no protocol change; 0.5.x clients and hubs keep interoperating. Hub schema changes are limited to additive, idempotent statements named in the child.
- Commandment 15: every user-visible change updates the agent-facing docs (child .8 hosts the shared sync skill; each child lists its doc delta in acceptance).
- Never put customer data, provider recommendations or exploit details into code, tests, comments, commits or tickets (tasks.json is a public export).
- Design record: internal-docs/ADR-006-SYNC-REPLICATION-CORE.md (maintainer-only, gitignored), sections cited per child. Reproduction scaffolding for S1-S7: internal-docs/repro/sync_replay_repro_test.go.txt.
nodes.acceptance:
1. Every child is done with its own acceptance met.
2. v0.5.4-beta is tagged from release/0.5.x with all release gates green (tests, race, coverage thresholds, lint, govulncheck, cloud-contract gate).
3. The security advisory for .1 is published with the release, not before.
4. release/0.5.x is merged into main; relay-side follow-ups on main are done.
5. CHANGELOG entry lists every fix and the new repair command.

nodes.title: Hub privilege hardening (0.5.x): owner-run, verified revocation; TRUNCATE guard; doctor check
nodes.description:
Hub tables are created unqualified in the connecting role's default schema, with no explicit privilege management. Depending on how a Postgres instance is provisioned, roles other than the mtix role can hold privileges on them. mtix must let an owner remove unintended access, verify the result, and report remaining exposure.

The first draft of this ticket was refuted by the independent review. It proposed row-level security with no policies and revocation on every push. The review found that this silently empties pulls for legitimate non-owner roles, that a REVOKE run by a non-grantor is a silent no-op, and that DDL on every push takes AccessExclusive locks.

Maintainer detail: ADR-006 D26; review F-03, F-19, F-20, F-44, F-72 (internal-docs/reviews/ADR-006-FR-23-review-2026-09-23.md). Do not copy scenario details into public artifacts before the advisory ships.
nodes.prompt:
Files: internal/store/postgres/transport (new hub_privileges.go), migrate.go, cmd/mtix (new `mtix sync harden`), cmd/mtix/sync_doctor.go.
1. Table list: derive it from the embedded migrations. Export the helper for .7's backup coverage.
2. Do NOT enable row-level security in 0.5.x (F-03).
3. `mtix sync harden` is dry-run by default; `--apply` changes privileges. It is owner-only: refuse with a clear message and exit non-zero unless current_user owns every sync table. Runs only on explicit request, never on push. Remove every privilege on the sync tables, their sequences and mtix functions from:
   - PUBLIC;
   - the data-API role names listed in ADR-006 section 4.1 item 10;
   - every other non-owner role not named with `--keep-role <name>` (repeatable). Dry-run lists these roles first, so an operator never revokes a legitimate team role by surprise.
   Then revoke the matching DEFAULT privileges (ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE <creator> IN SCHEMA <schema> …) wherever the caller is allowed to; otherwise report them as remaining exposure.
4. Verify, and treat a WARNING as failure. Afterwards, for every role in pg_roles other than the owner, kept roles and superusers, check has_table_privilege(role, table, priv) for SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES and TRIGGER. This catches predefined roles and membership, which role_table_grants misses. Any true value = FAIL. A REVOKE that raises a PostgreSQL WARNING also fails the command.
5. Append-only guard: add BEFORE TRUNCATE … FOR EACH STATEMENT triggers that raise on audit_log, sync_conflicts and sync_events. Create them only when absent (check pg_trigger first) to avoid needless AccessExclusive locks (F-44). Row triggers never fire on TRUNCATE.
6. `sync init`: run the same steps only when the caller is the owner, and only when the verification fails; issue no DDL when the hub is already clean. Push is untouched.
7. Doctor check `hub-privileges`, using the same verification: FAIL on any non-owner, non-kept privilege or a missing TRUNCATE guard; report trigger state (tgenabled); give exact guidance (`mtix sync harden`); support --json. Coordinate with MTIX-93.
8. SQL rules: identifiers cannot be bound parameters. Build each statement server-side with `SELECT format('REVOKE ALL ON TABLE %I.%I FROM %I', $1, $2, $3)` using bound arguments, then execute the returned text. Go never concatenates identifiers.
9. Advisory: draft it in internal-docs in capability wording (no provider names, F-72): who is affected, how to check, how to fix. Publish with the release (.9).
10. Agent docs: the hub-privileges section of the mtix-sync skill (.8.1).
nodes.acceptance:
Real Postgres (local MTIX_PG_TEST_DSN; cloud-contract gate in CI), red-first:
1. TestHarden_RevokesUnintendedAccess. Fixture: PUBLIC grants, the data-API roles from ADR-006 4.1.10, an unrelated role, a member of a predefined read-all role, and default privileges that re-grant future tables. After harden --apply --keep-role <team role>, verification passes, the kept role still works, and a table created afterwards is not readable by the API roles (or is reported as remaining exposure).
2. TestHarden_NonOwner_RefusesWithoutChanges.
3. TestHarden_RevokeWarningIsFailure (non-grantor case).
4. TestTruncateGuard_BlocksOwnerTruncate on all three tables.
5. TestHarden_CleanHub_NoDDL, and TestPush_IssuesNoDDL.
6. TestDoctorHubPrivileges: FAIL before, PASS after; --json fields present.
7. No row-level security enabled anywhere.
8. Advisory draft in capability wording.

nodes.title: Workflow events apply by last-writer-wins at ingest (claim, unclaim, transition, defer)
nodes.description: Today claim, unclaim, transition_status and defer events apply unconditionally at ingest. Any late or older workflow event therefore reverts newer state, whatever its source: own replay, the late-event sweep (.5), out-of-order relay delivery, or a teammate's concurrent event. Phase 0 applies at ingest the same winner rule that the repair tool (.6) uses offline. Review F-43, F-28.
nodes.prompt:
Files: internal/store/sqlite/sync_apply.go, plus a new file sync_workflow_winner.go shared with .6.
Rule: a workflow event applies only if its key K = (lamport_clock, wall_clock_ts, author_machine_hash ascending, event_id) beats every workflow event already held for the same node. Scope by uid, falling back to node_id, as detectLWWOutcome does. Workflow events are transition_status, claim, unclaim, defer, and update_field on status, assignee, agent_state and defer_until.
A losing event is still mirrored and recorded as applied, but changes no node column. A winning event writes exactly the columns its local mutation writes. Derive that table from transition.go, claim.go and the defer path, and keep it as one documented constant table in code. closed_at comes from the winning event's wall_clock_ts when the status is terminal.
Known residual, to document: secondary columns (for example, an assignee set by an earlier claim) can differ from a strict K-order replay when events arrive out of order. Full convergence arrives with the phase-4 projector.
Coordinate with .2 (the same apply path; land .2 first).
